payload.title: The Cardinal Compass Turn
payload.promptText: Observe how the arrow moves across the four positions in the sequence.
payload.observationPrompt: What do you notice changing as you look from left to right?

observationChoices.label: The direction the arrow is pointing
The number of arrows in the box

ruleOptions.label: The arrow turns 90° clockwise (a quarter turn to the right) each step.
The arrow flips upside down back and forth.
The arrow changes to point toward random corners.

hints.name: Attention
hints.content: Focus only on the sharp tip of the arrow. Which way does it point in each box?

hints.name: Relationship
hints.content: Notice how the arrow turns just like the hands on a wall clock—one quarter turn each step.

hints.name: Guided Demonstration
hints.content: From Step 3 pointing Down (180°), another 90° clockwise turn makes it point Left (270°).

explanationSteps: In Step 1, the arrow points straight up towards 12 o'clock (0°).
In Step 2, it makes a 90° clockwise quarter-turn to point right (3 o'clock).
In Step 3, it turns another 90° clockwise to point straight down (6 o'clock).
Following this invariant rule, the missing fourth position must turn 90° clockwise once more to point left (9 o'clock).

transferChallenge.prompt: Apply the same 90° clockwise rotation rule to this new problem with triangles.

payload.pedagogicalTakeaway: Rotations preserve shape and size while altering cardinal orientation systematically.

feedback.obs-dir: Yes, that changes from step to step.
feedback.obs-col: Look again. Does this really change?
feedback.obs-siz: Look again. Does this really change?
feedback.obs-cnt: Look again. Does this really change?

feedback.rule-90-cw: Up (0°) turns right to 90°, then down to 180°, and finally left to 270°.
feedback.rule-flip: Notice that step 2 points horizontally to the right, which is not an upside-down flip.
feedback.rule-random: The change follows an exact clockwise pattern, like hands on a clock.

feedback.opt-a: Correct! The vertex points left (270°), completing the 90° clockwise rotation cycle.
feedback.opt-b: This points upward (0°), which skips the 270° position.
feedback.opt-c: This is identical to Step 3, with no rotation applied.
feedback.opt-d: This points right, which was Step 2.

accessibility_metadata.alt: The Cardinal Compass Turn: Observe how the arrow moves across the four positions in the sequence.

payload.pedagogicalTakeaway: Distinguishing clockwise from counterclockwise requires comparing consecutive transitions.

payload.title: The Mirror Flag
payload.promptText: Watch how the flag flips across a mirror line in the middle.
payload.observationPrompt: What happens to the flag between Step 1 and Step 2?

observationChoices.label: It turns around like a wheel

ruleOptions.label: The shape reflects horizontally across a vertical mirror line each step.
The shape rotates 180 degrees.

hints.name: Attention
hints.content: Look at the top of the pole. Does the flag stay at the top, or move to the bottom?

hints.name: Relationship
hints.content: Because top stays at the top while left becomes right, this is a horizontal reflection (flip).

hints.name: Guided Demonstration
hints.content: Reflect the shape horizontally across the vertical axis.

explanationSteps: Reflection flips an object across a mirror line without rotating.
In a horizontal reflection across a vertical mirror, the Y coordinates remain fixed while X coordinates invert.
Step 1 points right, Step 2 points left, Step 3 points right, so Step 4 must point left.

transferChallenge.prompt: Select the horizontally reflected counterpart of this asymmetric arrow.

payload.pedagogicalTakeaway: Mirror reflections invert chirality; no pure rotation in the plane can replicate a reflection of an asymmetric shape.

feedback.rule-flip-h: The flag points right, then left, then right again, like looking into a mirror.
feedback.rule-rot-180: If it turned 180°, the flag would hang at the bottom of its pole. Here the flag stays at the top.

feedback.opt-ref-a: Correct! Horizontal reflection of an arrow pointing right turns it pointing left.
feedback.opt-ref-b: Pointing up is a rotation, not a reflection.

accessibility_metadata.alt: The Mirror Flag: Watch how the flag flips across a mirror line in the middle.

payload.title: Reflection or Rotation? (The Chiral Test)
payload.promptText: One of the most common pitfalls on reasoning tests is confusing rotation with reflection.
payload.observationPrompt: Can this transformation be achieved by merely rotating the shape, or does it require a reflection?

observationChoices.label: It must be a reflection because chiral handedness changed
It can be solved by turning 90 degrees

ruleOptions.label: Horizontal reflection. No amount of 2D rotation can match this figure.
Rotation of 180 degrees.

hints.name: Attention
hints.content: Try using the rotation buttons in the experiment canvas. Can you get the flag to match the target?

hints.name: Relationship
hints.content: Turning 180° puts the flag at the bottom of the pole. Only a left-right flip keeps it at the top while changing which way it points.

hints.name: Guided Demonstration
hints.content: Use the Flip ↔ button to solve it.

explanationSteps: Therefore, a flipped flag cannot be made by turning alone.

transferChallenge.prompt: Shape A is flipped left to right, like in a mirror. Which picture shows the result?

payload.pedagogicalTakeaway: The "point-test" (tracking an asymmetrical marker or tip) reliably distinguishes reflection from rotation.

feedback.obs-must-reflect: Yes, that changes from step to step.
feedback.obs-can-rotate: Look again. Does this really change?

feedback.rule-must-reflect: Try turning the flag 90°, 180° or 270°. It never matches the target without a flip.
feedback.rule-can-turn: Turn it 180° and test it: the flag ends up hanging at the bottom of the pole, unlike the target.

feedback.opt-chiral-ref: Yes. The foot of the L now points the other way and nothing else changed. Only a flip can do that.
feedback.opt-chiral-rot: This is a half turn, not a flip. Turn your hand over and compare: the L would be upside down.
feedback.opt-chiral-quarter: This was turned a quarter turn. Turning keeps the same handedness, so it cannot be the mirror image.
feedback.opt-chiral-same: This is the same as Shape A. Nothing was flipped.

accessibility_metadata.alt: Reflection or Rotation? (The Chiral Test): One of the most common pitfalls on reasoning tests is confusing rotation with reflection.

payload.title: Distractor Shield (Invariant vs Noisy Attributes)
payload.promptText: Filter out the distracting noise to find which rule actually matters.
payload.observationPrompt: Which property is governed by a consistent, predictable rule?

observationChoices.label: The direction rotates in regular 90° steps; color changes are random

ruleOptions.label: Orientation is the only true rule (90° clockwise). The colors are non-rule distractors.
Color is predictable.

hints.name: Attention
hints.content: Ignore the colors completely and look only at the pointing direction.

hints.name: Relationship
hints.content: Up, Right, Down: the next rotation must point Left (270°).

hints.name: Guided Demonstration
hints.content: Rotate to 270° pointing Left.

explanationSteps: Standardized visual reasoning assessments (CogAT / NNAT) often include irrelevant visual variations.
Learning to suppress distractor cues is a hallmark of mature visual reasoning.

transferChallenge.prompt: Identify the shape that satisfies the true orientation rule, ignoring background color.

payload.pedagogicalTakeaway: Distractor suppression is the cognitive ability to filter irrelevant visual noise.
